extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers of Montaigne; readers interested in essays on marriage, sex, and morals
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / interpretation of Montaigne's essay material discussing marriage, love, chastity, and social customs; contains normative observations and examples rather than a formal checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe the laws of marriage / manage liberty prudently
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis in vain to kick, when a man has once put on his fetters: a man must prudently manage his liberty; but having once submitted to obligation, he must confine himself within the laws of common duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once married one should accept the obligations of the contract and behave within the bounds of common duty. The essay treats submission to marriage as requiring prudent self-limitation rather than continual resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not enter marriage with hatred or contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: They who engage in this contract, with a design to carry themselves in it with hatred and contempt, do an unjust and inconvenient thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entering marriage while intending enmity or disdain is morally wrong and practically harmful. The author contrasts hostile, dissembling behaviour (the quoted women’s maxim: “Serve thy husband as thy master, but guard thyself against him as from a traitor”) as an injurious anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage requires espousal of duty, not mere formality
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man does not always perform his duty, he ought at least to love and acknowledge it; ‘tis treachery to marry without espousing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne distinguishes mere formal marriage from the genuine acceptance of marital duty — to marry without embracing the associated obligations is a kind of betrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate marriage and love as distinct ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage has utility, justice, honour, and constancy for its share; a flat, but more universal pleasure: love founds itself wholly upon pleasure, and, indeed, has it more full, lively, and sharp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic expectations: marriage supplies stability and social goods, while romantic love supplies intense pleasure and volatility. The two goals can overlap but are conceptually distinct and should be treated as such when judging conduct and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that external passion need not wholly negate duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A woman may give the reins to her own passion, and yield to the importunities of love, and yet reserve some duty toward marriage, and that it may be hurt, without being totally broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne allows gradations: infidelity or yielding to passion can coexist with retained duties; one should avoid simplistic, all-or-nothing moral judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unreasonable double standards about women’s chastity and vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: We, on the contrary, would have them at once sound, vigorous plump, high-fed, and chaste; that is to say, both hot and cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticizes societal expectations that demand contradictory qualities (sexual vigor and absolute chastity) and marks such standards as unfair and unworkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorious interdiction often increases curiosity and vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The woman... stopped her short a little roughly, and made her skip over that dangerous step... I let her alone, not to trouble their rules... the commerce of twenty lacquies could not... have so imprinted in her memory the meaning... as this good old woman did by reprimand and interdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibitions and harsh reprimands can backfire by making forbidden topics more attractive; gentler handling or information may be preferable to strict interdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty (when not crabbed) is a powerful allure
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no allurement like modesty, if it be not rude and crabbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modesty enhances attraction provided it is sincere and not offensively distant; Montaigne contrasts this with crude impudence and suggests modest behaviour yields greater esteem and desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and praise the difficulty of maintaining chastity
rubrics_metrics.description: I hold it more easy to carry a suit of armour all the days of one’s life than a maidenhead; and the vow of virginity of all others is the most noble, as being the hardest to keep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize chastity as an active, difficult achievement; praise and esteem for constancy are warranted because the restraint is arduous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow a neutral frontier of conduct — small relaxations need not be fault
rubrics_metrics.description: The limits of honour are not cut so short; they may give themselves a little rein, and relax a little without being faulty: there lies on the frontier some space free, indifferent, and neuter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues for tolerance of minor, non-harmful relaxations of strict honour codes rather than immediate moral condemnation; judge by context and degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and opportunity are decisive in matters of love
rubrics_metrics.description: what was the first thing to be considered in love matters, I should answer that it was how to take a fitting time; and so the second; and so the third—‘tis a point that can do everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success or failure in amour often depends more on choosing the right moment and circumstances than on sheer desire or boldness; prudence and timing are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Men should preserve reverence and bashfulness in courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: I would in this affair have a man a little play the child, the timorous, and the servant... he who in this traffic takes away the reverence, defaces at the same time the lustre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive boldness or contempt reduces attraction; courteous, modest, or somewhat deferential behaviour is recommended in pursuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bragging about sexual exploits is foolish and damaging
rubrics_metrics.description: There is neither continency nor virtue where there are no opposing desires... a gentleman... to justify himself, went about boldly swearing that he had ridden twenty stages the night before: an oath that was afterwards made use of to convict him of his ignorance in that affair, and to divorce him from his wife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boasting can expose one to ridicule and harm reputation; self-protective modesty is wiser than bragging about sexual activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive punishment and austerity worsen the vice they aim to prevent
rubrics_metrics.description: The austerity of our decrees renders the application of women to this vice more violent and vicious than its own condition needs, and engages it in consequences worse than their cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harsh legal or social penalties can produce perverse incentives (e.g., pushing women to public lawsuits or other desperate acts) and therefore moderation and wise policy are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jealousy is a damaging and often foolish passion
rubrics_metrics.description: This our immoderate and illegitimate exasperation against this vice springs from the most vain and turbulent disease that afflicts human minds, which is jealousy... she, and envy, her sister, seem to me to be the most foolish of the whole troop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne treats jealousy as self-destructive, likely to produce worse outcomes; it should be recognized and checked rather than indulged.
